episode_thesis: Tom Babbage argues that a commodity-only alternative-markets trend program earns its place through structural market selection, not backtest selection: physically distinct, little-speculated commodities have more independent risk, better trend drift and better trend autocorrelation because supply and demand are inelastic and hedgers dominate, provided capacity stays small enough to allocate meaningfully to niche markets. He adds that execution is a second source of edge: giving the trading desk a tracking-error budget to wait passively behaves like an anti-trend buffer, cuts slippage close to zero relative to prior years and permits faster signals.

speakers.name: Tom Babbage
speakers.role: Chief scientist, Gresham Investment Management; runs the AQA alternative-commodity trend program (ex-Winton researcher, astrophysics PhD)

worldview_premises.premise: Diversification comes from effective degrees of freedom, not market count; beyond a few hundred markets the next one has a tiny allocation and changes nothing, and related instruments (2-, 5-, 10-year Treasuries) are one market.

Financialized markets (FX, indices, fixed income) collapse to one in macro shocks, whereas less financialized commodities with distinct regional, consumer and producer drivers stay independent and resilient.
worldview_premises.support: Structural description plus examples (sunflower seeds, US East Coast power, Chinese bitumen); not quantified in the talk.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity trends have a structural cause: inelastic supply and demand, long permitting, shipping and storage frictions mean imbalances clear only via large persistent price moves.
worldview_premises.support: Coal mine example; no tests shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend splits into drift (quantity) and autocorrelation (quality), and both are better in low-speculation alternative commodities than mainstream ones over about 30 years.
worldview_premises.support: Internal paper 'You Trend, I'll Follow'; a measured gap over 30 years.

worldview_premises.premise: Deferred contracts (about 5 years out) are dominated by hedgers and trend more smoothly than the speculative, news-driven front.
worldview_premises.support: Analogy of news and weather vs climate.

worldview_premises.premise: Selecting markets by backtest Sharpe is data mining and the key to future misery; selection should rest on market structure.
worldview_premises.support: Claims it is classic systematic finance failure since parameter search is cheap; example of carbon.

worldview_premises.premise: Alternativeness means low correlation to mainstream commodities and few speculators, not low liquidity or access barriers.
worldview_premises.support: A low-liquidity oil spread correlated with crude is just costly crude exposure.

worldview_premises.premise: Capacity discipline is what keeps a commodity book diversified: at billions, allocation concentrates in crude, gold and gas and niche markets cease to matter.
Execution risk is a small share of portfolio variance, so cost savings from passive execution dominate any risk it adds.
worldview_premises.support: At 15% annual risk, trades are about 5% of daily variance and uncorrelated across markets.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodity prices and inflation are two sides of the same coin, so commodity trend is convex to both inflation and deflation regimes.
worldview_premises.support: Goods are commodities; cites the firm's 'Eras Tour' paper adding commodity trend to 60/40.

worldview_premises.premise: Signals with clear structural drivers survive long drawdowns, while opaque machine-learning signals are pulled after three weak years.
worldview_premises.support: Client behaviour observed by the firm.

decision_process.practice: Trade about 150 markets, rotating roughly a quarter per year (44 dropped, 31 added in 2025), chosen on market structure: who trades, where on the curve, correlation to mainstream commodities, speculator share (COT, open interest to delivery, broker queries, conference attendance).
Cluster markets by shared physical drivers (a furnace cluster of iron ore, flat glass, coking coal) to manage correlation and risk.
decision_process.why: Real supply-chain linkages, not only statistical estimates.

decision_process.practice: Avoid markets that have become financialized (cocoa) and avoid the front of the oil curve; accept an asset without a prior trend record (EU carbon with negative 8-year trend Sharpe was included in 2016 and became a top performer).
decision_process.why: Selection on structure rather than backtest.

decision_process.practice: Treat long and short symmetrically, but override the model to stop adding to shorts near a price floor (California carbon auction floor).

Position proportional to signal strength (several trend horizons) and inversely proportional to volatility; largest position set so it can be exited in about a week in stress; new markets start small until real fills confirm costs.
decision_process.why: Liquidity and diversification determine top-line capacity.

decision_process.practice: Soft-close capacity (half-closed around 1bn; top line a couple of billion), leaving headroom after a 15-20% year.
decision_process.why: Multi-year trend horizon; protect existing clients.

decision_process.practice: Give the desk a tracking-error budget to work orders passively over several days within bounds; never trade against the model or on own views; fall back to normal trading when the limit is hit.
decision_process.why: Avoid crossing the spread, anti-correlated buffer, faster signals possible.

decision_process.practice: Use a wide network of specialist brokers and dealers by phone quotes; onboard new brokers when adding markets; access Chinese futures via swaps with margin held by a third party; all others are exchange-cleared futures.
decision_process.why: Niche markets cannot be plugged electronically; competition on pricing.

decision_process.practice: Position the program as a diversifying addition (20-25% correlation to the SG CTA index) beside cheap liquid core trend, not as the equity-shock convexity core.
decision_process.why: Core trend with equity-shock convexity should come from cheap liquid trend.

speakers.evidence_style: Structural first principles and market microstructure (who trades, where on the curve), supported by internal papers (drift/autocorrelation, Eras Tour, The Waiting Game) and a year of live execution results; explicitly rejects backtest Sharpe as a selection criterion. Examples are single cases (EU carbon, cocoa, propane).

current_views.view: Alternative-commodity trend has been through a multi-year drawdown, which he attributes to sampling the weaker side of a long-run positive Sharpe distribution.
current_views.reasoning: Structural logic (inelastic supply, concrete diversification) lets investors hold through it.

current_views.view: The book was up in April 2025 around the Liberation Day shock, confirming that niche commodities follow their own drivers rather than risk-on/risk-off.
current_views.reasoning: Insulation from the financial risk factor.

current_views.view: Macro themes the book taps through capacity discipline: biofuels and green transition, uranium for AI data-centre power, freight routes and onshoring, tariff wars.
current_views.reasoning: Different regions' supply, demand and logistics are diverging.

current_views.view: Cocoa 2024 was the biggest commodity trend after 20 years without a trend, yet too financialized to trade.
current_views.reasoning: Illustrates trend appearing without prior history and the financialization screen.

positions.speaker: Tom Babbage
positions.position: Beyond a few hundred markets another changes nothing; what matters is real independence and capacity discipline.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Claims of better drift and autocorrelation in alternative commodities rest on an internal paper; no magnitudes or out-of-sample test are given, and the market classification was made by the firm (selection risk).

Argues backtest-based market selection is data mining, but market selection by 'alternativeness' also uses long history to document the drift and autocorrelation gap; EU carbon is a single post-hoc success example.

Reports near-zero slippage over just over one year, with admitted higher slippage variance and anecdotal propane evidence; the gain relative to prior years is not quantified and may be luck or regime.

Says a 10bn book would look like a standard commodity allocation while also saying 4-5bn capacity was possible on paper during COVID; the capacity ceiling depends on volatility and prices and is judgemental.
Avoids cocoa as too financialized despite the biggest commodity trend in 2024, which tests the financialization screen against its opportunity cost.
Inflation convexity claim relies on a firm paper; the instruments and period of the 60/40 test are not described.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs named that lead future trend opportunities: speculator participation in a market (COT, share of open interest delivered, entry of other CTAs), position on the curve (deferred contracts), supply inelasticity, physical clusters (furnace chain), structural themes (biofuels, uranium, freight, onshoring, tariffs) and regime of high commodity volatility (raises dollar-risk capacity). Horizon is multi-year; he does not offer a price forecast.
reader_inferences: (reader) The financialization screen implies that alternative-market edge decays as more CTAs enter, so Babbage's own program is exposed to crowding of the markets he identifies as alternative.

(reader) Capacity measured in dollar risk means that the same assets under management can be fully invested or oversized depending on the commodity volatility regime; a model of CTA capacity should include volatility.

(reader) Passive execution converts part of the execution budget into an implicit short-horizon mean-reversion position, which is why he can speak of raising the risk scale; the same logic would fail in trending, gapping markets.
(reader) The claim that commodity trend is convex to both inflation and deflation is an interpretation of goods prices as commodity prices and is testable against CPI components.
